title: Hypothermia-Associated Loss of Dendritic Spines
abstract: Mechanisms of synaptic plasticity in CNS circuits are commonly investigated using in vitro preparations such as brain slices or slice culture. During their preparation, slices are exposed to low temperatures, and electrophysiological measurements are sometimes made below physiological temperature. Because dendritic spines, which occur at the majority of excitatory synapses, are morphologically plastic, we investigated the influence of reduced temperature on their morphology and plasticity using live cell imaging of hippocampal slices from transgenic mice expressing a green fluorescent protein-based neuronal surface marker and electron microscopy of adult brain slices. Our data show that dendritic spines are highly sensitive to reduced temperature with rapid loss of actin-based motility followed at longer times by reversible loss of the entire spine structure. Thus, reduced temperature significantly affects synaptic morphology, which is in turn known to influence several key aspects of synaptic transmission. Evidence that hypothermia potentiates anesthesia and is associated with spine loss in hibernating animals further suggests that spine morphology may have a widespread influence on brain function.

Full narrative

Hypothermia-Associated Loss of Dendritic Spines (2004) in Journal of Neuroscience is authored by Martijn Roelandse and Andrew Matus. Topics: Dendritic spine, Hippocampal formation, Neuroscience, Dendritic filopodia and Biology.

55 citations (OpenAlex). Citations peaked in 2006 with 11 citing works. Citing venues include Journal of Neuroscience, Neuroscience and Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience.

Limited online visibility beyond citations.
narrative_llm:
Short impact summary

This 2004 Journal of Neuroscience article has become a recognizable reference point in synaptic plasticity research, with 55 OpenAlex citations, 56 documented downstream reuses, and evidence of continued scholarly attention across reviews and later experimental papers. Its influence is especially clear in work on temperature-sensitive synaptic structure, hibernation/torpor biology, and dendritic spine plasticity.

Full narrative

Roelandse and Matus addressed a practical but important methodological question: what happens to dendritic spines when brain tissue is exposed to reduced temperature during slice preparation and electrophysiology? By linking hypothermia to spine morphology in the hippocampal formation, the paper helped clarify that the experimental conditions commonly used to study synaptic plasticity can themselves alter the structures being measured. That framing gave the study lasting relevance well beyond its immediate technical context.

The citation record shows steady scholarly uptake over time rather than a single burst of attention. The article has 55 citations in OpenAlex, appears in a strong percentile position for its record, and is reused by 56 downstream works spanning articles, reviews, dissertations, a book chapter, a preprint, and a peer-review record. Its citation neighborhood is concentrated in neuroscience venues, with recurring appearances in journals such as Journal of Neuroscience, Neuroscience, Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience, Journal of Neuroscience Methods, and Experimental Neurology, indicating that the paper has served as a practical and conceptual touchstone within the field.

The thematic spread of citing work is also telling. Later papers use the study in discussions of dendritic spine plasticity, synaptic structure under temperature change, neuroprotection, torpor, and hibernation-inspired biology. Recent citations include reviews and experimental articles that explicitly connect synaptic plasticity with body temperature and natural torpor, showing that the paper’s relevance has extended into broader questions about brain state, metabolic suppression, and structural stability in neurons. In that sense, the article has become part of the evidentiary base for thinking about temperature as a regulator of synaptic form and function.

Public and community discussion is modest in the available record, with only a small number of tracked mentions and no visible scite supporting or contradicting statements captured here. That relative quiet does not diminish the paper’s academic footprint; rather, it suggests that its impact has been primarily technical and scholarly, spreading through citation, reuse, and incorporation into later synthesis. The open-access record also shows multiple accessible instances, which likely aided continued uptake and reuse over time.
